first.rationale: The two declining metrics (onboarding completion -4%, activation -6%) are causally linked: onboarding is upstream of activation, so a fix there can move both, whereas activation messaging treats only the downstream symptom. memory_86 (shortened onboarding lifted completion and time-to-value) and memory_31 (fewer signup fields lifted first-week activation durably) both point at this lever, and memory_31's 'durable' framing matters for the sustainable-revenue objective. I am deliberately not taking the competitor bait: memory_73 records that promotional pricing buys acquisition at the cost of 30-day retention and explicitly warns against generalizing it, so matching entry pricing would trade long-term qualified revenue for a short-term defensive win. Referral incentives (memory_57) are clean but act on established customers and do nothing for the two metrics that are actually bleeding; enterprise sales-assist (memory_44) is a different segment entirely and cannot be stood up meaningfully in one week. I spend verification on memory_86 because it is the primary load-bearing claim for my choice and I need to know whether the reported lift was in completion rate alone or carried through to retained, paying accounts, and on memory_91 because it is the strongest alternative for the activation drop -- if its week-one engagement gain turned out to be durable revenue rather than a click-through artifact, I would switch. I do not verify memory_31: it is corroborating rather than decisive, and it is the oldest record (day 12), so a 76-day-old signup-flow finding may no longer describe the current product regardless of what the archive says. Key downstream risk I am carrying explicitly: lowering onboarding friction can inflate completion and activation counts by admitting lower-intent accounts, which would show as a metric win while qualified revenue flat-lines or degrades. I therefore want the experiment instrumented on 30-day retention and revenue quality, not completion rate, and I am running at standard scale rather than broad rollout because none of the inherited results were measured against the current competitive environment, and the observed declines may share an external cause that no onboarding change will address.

final.rationale: Verification resolved my main worry about memory_86 in its favor: the shortened onboarding flow did not just inflate a completion counter, it moved 30-day retention +3% and cut time-to-value by 2.1 days. That is the retained-value signature I was looking for, and it substantially defuses the low-intent-admission risk I flagged -- if the friction reduction were merely letting unqualified accounts through, retention would have gone flat or negative, not up. memory_31 corroborates directionally, though I still discount it as the oldest record. exp_91 also came back confirmed and is genuinely strong (activation +6%, retention +1%), and I note its activation lift numerically matches the exact 6% decline I am facing, which is superficially seductive. I am still not choosing it, for two reasons: onboarding sits upstream of activation, so fixing completion plausibly recovers part of the activation drop as a second-order effect while the reverse is not true; and exp_86's retention effect is three times larger, which is what the sustainable-qualified-revenue objective actually keys on. Activation messaging is my clear second choice and the right follow-up next slot. I continue to decline promotional_pricing despite the competitor's entry pricing -- memory_73's retention damage and its explicit do-not-generalize warning make it a direct trade against the stated objective, and matching a price attack with a retention-destroying instrument compounds the problem rather than solving it. Referral incentive and enterprise sales-assist address neither declining metric on this timescale. Remaining uncertainty I am not papering over: both verified experiments predate the competitor launch, so their effect sizes were measured in a calmer market and may not replicate at the same magnitude now; the QoQ declines could also share an external driver that no onboarding change touches. Standard experiment rather than broad rollout for exactly that reason, with the readout gated on 30-day retention and qualified revenue rather than completion rate, so that a repeat of the exp_86 result is confirmed under current conditions before anything ships wide.
